report.scope: Real appellation-controlled Champagne from France, roughly $30–$250. Cava, Prosecco and American "champagne" excluded. No current retail prices confirmed; 2019 Wine Enthusiast prices are a relative floor only.

primer.what_it_is: Sparkling wine from France's Champagne region, made by traditional method (second fermentation in bottle). Bottle price mostly reflects brand, distribution margin and allocation, not liquid quality.

must_haves.why: Legally protected name, so it means real Champagne
Second fermentation in bottle; automatic for real Champagne
Producer code (NM, RM, CM, MA) in label fine print predicts quality best
Brut Nature or Extra Brut shows quality naked; Sec and Demi-Sec hide flaws
Provenance matters more than any spec; heat and light ruin bottles

premium_features.why: Single harvest year; adds rarity and ageing
A house's top bottling (e.g. Dom Pérignon); mostly pays for age, allocation and brand

avoid.why: Add cost for packaging, flutes or ice buckets, not wine
Cheap "Champagne-style" wines and unverifiable sub-$30 unknowns may be thin or mass-market
Old stock in light and heat is worth less than nothing

verdict.headline: Buy selectively: grower Champagne at the $50–70 knee beats famous names at full price.
verdict.confidence: Low to moderate: no current retail prices verified; knee is the author's judgment.
verdict.reasoning: Experts and sommeliers agree growers beat big brands on value. Knee is about $50–70 for non-vintage grower or small-house bottles. Skip full-price famous NV, gift boxes and young prestige cuvées. Thresholds are provisional.
verdict.price_watch_summary: Big-house NV: buy about 15–20% under shelf, wait for November–December case promotions. Growers: buy at or under about $50–65; Lassaigne at $70–80 is fair. Kirkland, Aldi, Trader Joe's rarely discount. Prestige and vintage rarely discount.

normalization.unit: Dollars per quality-adjusted pour you will actually enjoy
normalization.unit_rationale: Naive $/750 ml bottle misleads: quality varies hugely within a fixed volume, so two $60 bottles can differ by two quality tiers. Per-use equals per-pour since Champagne is consumed in one sitting.
normalization.quality_adjustment: Quality-adjusted price = shelf price ÷ Q, Q from 0.6 to 1.6. Built from five factors: producer type (NM, RM, CM, MA), time on lees (15 months legal minimum for NV, good bottles 30+), dosage, reserve wine share, base vintage and disgorgement date. Working assumption: grower RM at $50–70 delivers about the same enjoyment as NM house bottle at $75–100.
normalization.size_economics: A 1.5 L magnum costs about the same or a bit more per ml but ages better. Buy magnums only for cellaring or large events.

diminishing_returns.knee_example: Grower or small-house NV at $50–70, e.g. Drappier Brut Nature (~$50) and Lassaigne ($70–80), rated star value picks by VinePair sommeliers.
diminishing_returns.below_knee: At about $30–45 you give up lees time, get more dosage masking and thinner reserve wine. Real Champagne but plainer; sub-$30 bottles need storage confirmed.
diminishing_returns.above_knee: Money buys vintage rarity, grand cru terroir, longer ageing and brand status. A $200+ prestige bottle is not 3× the pleasure of a $65 grower bottle for most drinkers.

spec_criteria.what_good_looks_like: RM (grower) usually better quality per dollar; NM consistent but marketing-heavy; MA is the cheap store label
spec_criteria.why_it_matters: Top predictor of quality. Working assumption: RM at $50–70 ≈ NM house bottle at $75–100

spec_criteria.why_it_matters: Shows how fresh the bottle is; old oxidized bottles can be worth near zero

spec_criteria.what_good_looks_like: Extra Brut or Brut Nature; Brut covers most bottles; Sec and Demi-Sec hide flaws
spec_criteria.why_it_matters: Very dry wines show quality naked, with nothing to hide behind

spec_criteria.spec: Vintage or Grand Cru/Premier Cru village
spec_criteria.what_good_looks_like: Named vintage or classified village; lees time of 30+ months (legal NV minimum 15) and higher reserve-wine share are also good
spec_criteria.how_to_check: Label; many growers disclose lees time, few houses disclose reserve share
spec_criteria.why_it_matters: Shows where grapes came from, but partly marketing

spec_criteria.what_good_looks_like: Bottles kept cool and out of light, with good turnover
spec_criteria.how_to_check: Ask the retailer; avoid warm-shelf or sun-exposed bottles
spec_criteria.why_it_matters: Provenance matters more than any spec; heat and light ruin bottles

value_traps.instead: Grower RM bottles at $50–70; prestige cuvées last

tiers.who_its_for: Beginners wanting a safe baseline house style
tiers.verdict: $45–50 houses scored 90–91 in 2019; buy on promotion. Famous names at full price are not a value

tiers.who_its_for: Serious hobbyists seeking best value; restaurant buyers
tiers.verdict: Best value; De Sousa Caudalies scored 97 and Collet BdB 93 at $43 in 2019. Buy at or under about $50–65

tiers.who_its_for: Cellaring, or those wanting the specific bottle
tiers.verdict: Can be great but not 3× the pleasure of a $65 grower bottle; you pay for allocation and prestige. Rarely discounted

consensus.expert_view: Experts and sommeliers (VinePair, Wine Independent) agree grower bottles beat big brands on value; grower bottles at $50–100 rival big-brand vintage and prestige cuvées.
consensus.community_view: Not available: no Reddit thread could be retrieved, so no community consensus is reported.
consensus.where_they_disagree: Cannot be assessed without community data. The grower-over-brand view is a trade-press and sommelier view, not a verified consumer consensus.

caveats: No current retail price was confirmed for any product; retailer pages were blocked.
Most prices come from a December 2019 Wine Enthusiast list; Champagne prices have risen a lot since.
Only 2025 prices: Drappier Brut Nature ~$50, Lassaigne $70–80 (VinePair).
A price or buy_under of 0 means unconfirmed or no figure given; unit_price equals bottle price (750 ml).
Background figures (Veuve ~$60–80, Moët ~$50–60, prestige well above $200) are unverified.
Buy-under thresholds are provisional rules; check Wine-Searcher or a local store.
The $50–70 knee is the author's judgment, not verified against current prices.
Kirkland's sourcing from a known house is unverified.
Quality and value scores are comparative, relying on 2019 critic points where available.
No Reddit or community consensus retrieved; the growers-beat-big-brands view is trade-press and sommelier opinion.
Totals for purchase paths are rough and built on unverified prices.
Provenance and storage matter more than any spec; warm-shelf or old stock can be worth near zero.
